units.text: Notice that the wildcard must be enclosed in quotes in order to protect it from expansion by the shell.
units.sourceHTML: Notice that the wildcard must be enclosed in quotes in order to protect it from expansion by the shell.

units.text: As of findutils version 4.2.2 (2004), patterns for ‘⟦0⟧’ and ‘⟦1⟧’ match a file name with a leading ‘⟦2⟧’. For example the command ‘⟦3⟧’ match the file ⟦4⟧. Braces within the pattern (‘⟦5⟧’) are not considered to be special (that is, ⟦6⟧ matches a file named ⟦7⟧, not the files ⟦8⟧ and ⟦9⟧.
units.sourceHTML: As of findutils version 4.2.2 (2004), patterns for ‘-name’ and ‘-iname’ match a file name with a leading ‘.’. For example the command ‘find /tmp -name \*bar’ match the file /tmp/.foobar. Braces within the pattern (‘{}’) are not considered to be special (that is, find . -name 'foo{1,2}' matches a file named foo{1,2}, not the files foo1 and foo2.

units.text: Because the leading directories are removed, the file names considered for a match with ‘⟦0⟧’ will not include a slash (except for the root directory itself, ‘⟦1⟧’). So, ‘⟦2⟧’ will match the root directory, while ‘⟦3⟧’ will never match anything (you probably need to use ‘⟦4⟧’ instead).
units.sourceHTML: Because the leading directories are removed, the file names considered for a match with ‘-name’ will not include a slash (except for the root directory itself, ‘/’). So, ‘-name /’ will match the root directory, while ‘-name a/b’ will never match anything (you probably need to use ‘-path a/b’ instead).

units.text: The ‘⟦0⟧’ option appeared first in POSIX Issue 8 (IEEE Std 1003.1-2024) while GNU ⟦1⟧ supports it since version 3.8 (1993).
units.sourceHTML: The ‘-iname’ option appeared first in POSIX Issue 8 (IEEE Std 1003.1-2024) while GNU find supports it since version 3.8 (1993).
